definition: A health professional who cares for patients. Florence Nightingale made it a profession.
The beat felt in an artery each time the heart pumps. Usually 60 to 100 a minute at rest.
The skin of the head. It bleeds a lot when cut because of its rich blood supply.
The clear fluid left when blood clots. Many blood tests are run on it.
The light-and-lens tool for looking down the ear canal at the eardrum. ENT surgeons use a microscope for a closer look.
Relating to the ilium, the big wing-shaped bone of the pelvis.
The top vertebra, which holds up the skull, named after the Titan who held up the sky.
A break in the skin or tissue. Clean it, cover it, and watch for redness spreading.
Liquid waste made by the kidneys. Pale straw-coloured usually means well hydrated.
An air-filled space in the skull bones around the nose.
A poison made by a living thing, like tetanus toxin.
Optic nerve damage, often from raised eye pressure, that quietly steals side vision first. Regular eye checks from 40 catch it early. World Glaucoma Week.
An opening made on the belly so the bowel or bladder can empty into a bag.
A doctor filling in for another for a while. From the Latin locum tenens, place-holder.
The upper leg, home to the femur, the body’s longest and strongest bone.
Salty fluid that keeps the eyes moist. Emotional ones contain more protein.
A small mesh tube that props an artery open.
To wash thoroughly before surgery. Theatre scrubs went green and blue to cut glare and hide blood.
Brain disorder of overwhelming daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep attacks, sometimes with cataplexy: muscles going floppy with laughter or surprise. World Sleep Day.
Relating to the ulna, the forearm bone on the little-finger side.
Noisy breathing in sleep from a vibrating airway. Losing weight and sleeping on your side often help.
A beeper still carried in many hospitals because it’s so reliable.
Any liquid. About 60% of an adult’s body is water.
Short for streptococcus, the bacteria behind strep throat.
Slimy protective fluid lining the nose, airways and gut.
Tendency to repeated unprovoked seizures. Seizure first aid: time it, protect the head, nothing in the mouth, recovery position once it stops. Purple Day.
Big open-mouthed breaths that may help cool the brain. Contagious, even reading about them.
A finger or toe.
Sweet carbohydrate. Glucose is the brain’s main fuel.
A sudden rush of intense fear, with racing heart and breathlessness. Attacks pass within minutes.
A thin layer of sample spread on a slide. The old cervical test was called a Pap smear.
